hints: First translate the original DNA CCA TTC ACG GCG TTA GCA into its 6 amino acids using the table, so you know exactly what must stay the same.
Remember the genetic code is degenerate, so look for the option where both changed triplets still code for the same amino acids as the original (a silent mutation).
walkthrough:
**Translate the original sequence**

Great start, let us see what we are meant to make. Use the table triplet by triplet.

CCA = glycine, TTC = lysine, ACG = cysteine, GCG = arginine, TTA = asparagine, GCA = arginine. So the polypeptide is: gly - lys - cys - arg - asn - arg.

**Recall what no effect means**

A mutation has no effect if the amino acid sequence is unchanged. This happens because the code is degenerate, meaning several different triplets can code for the same amino acid. We need two base changes that are both silent.

**Test option B**

Option B is CCA TTC ACA GCA TTA GCA. Compare to the original. Only triplet 3 and triplet 4 are different. ACA is still cysteine like ACG, and GCA is still arginine like GCG. All six amino acids are identical, so the polypeptide is unchanged.

options.A: TTC (lysine) changes to ATC (STOP), which would terminate translation early, so this has a large effect even though TTA to TTG is silent.
options.B: ACG to ACA both code for cysteine and GCG to GCA both code for arginine, so both mutations are silent and the 6 amino acid sequence is unchanged.
options.C: GCG (arginine) changes to CCG (glycine), a missense change that alters the amino acid sequence, so it has an effect.
options.D: CCA to CCT is silent (both glycine) but GCA (arginine) to GGA (proline) changes the last amino acid, so it has an effect.
